country.name: Chile
country.tagline: A ribbon of vineyards between the Andes and a cold ocean, where phylloxera never arrived and a lost Bordeaux grape was found hiding in plain sight.

stats.note: SAG Catastro Vitícola 2024: 116,962 ha of wine grapes plus 9,287 ha of pisco grapes (OIV 2025 counts 154,000 ha including table grapes). Production: SAG 2026 harvest, 949.5 million litres excluding pisco wine. Rank: OIV 2025, where Chile made 8.4 mhl (8th).

country.overview:
Chile is a wine country shaped by walls. To the east the Andes rise above 6,000 m; to the west the cold Humboldt Current chills the Pacific; to the north lies the Atacama, the driest desert on Earth; to the south, ice fields and fjords. Inside that box, a strip rarely wider than 180 km and more than 1,300 km long from Copiapó to Chiloé, sits one of the most naturally protected vineyards in the world. Phylloxera, the root louse that destroyed Europe's vineyards in the late 19th century, has never established itself here, so most Chilean vines still grow on their own roots, and Chile's quarantine rules for plant material remain among the strictest of any wine country.

The geography also explains the climate. Between the Andes and the lower coastal range runs the Central Valley, a sun-soaked Mediterranean trough with dry summers and winter rain. Cold air drains off the mountains each night and the Pacific sends fog and wind through every gap in the coastal hills, so days are warm but nights are cool. That combination gives ripe fruit with real acidity and keeps disease pressure low. For most of the 20th century the industry worked the irrigated valley floor; since the 1980s it has moved outwards, east into the Andean foothills and west towards the coast, and Chileans now describe their wines by those bands as much as by valley: *Costa*, *Entre Cordilleras* and *Andes*.

Chilean wine has two founding stories. The first is colonial: Spanish conquistadors and missionaries brought the vine from Peru in the 1550s, and for three centuries Chile drank País, the grape known elsewhere as Mission or Listán Prieto, grown on dry hills in Maule and Itata. The second is French: from 1851, when Silvestre Ochagavía brought Bordeaux vines and a French winemaker to Santiago, the mining and banking elite planted Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Malbec and a then-common Bordeaux grape called Carmenère on estates around the capital. Phylloxera hit France soon after, so Chile kept vines that Europe lost, including Carmenère, which disappeared from Bordeaux and survived in Chile disguised as Merlot until the ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot identified it at Viña Carmen on 24 November 1994.

Modern Chilean wine dates from 1979, when Miguel Torres brought stainless steel and temperature control to Curicó, and from the export boom of the late 1980s and 1990s. Foreign investment followed: Lafite's Los Vascos, Mouton Rothschild's partnership with Concha y Toro in Almaviva, Robert Mondavi's with Errázuriz in Seña, and the Marnier-Lapostolle family in Apalta. In 2004 the Berlin Tasting placed Viñedo Chadwick 2000 and Seña 2001 above first-growth Bordeaux in a blind panel, a stunt that permanently changed Chile's image.

Today Chile is one of the world's largest exporters by volume, and its industry is in an uncomfortable transition. The national vineyard has shrunk from about 145,000 ha in 2020 to 126,000 ha in SAG's 2024 census, as falling global demand forces growers to pull out bulk vineyards, and 2026 production recovered to about 950 million litres after very short 2024 and 2025 crops. At the same time the country's most interesting wines have never been more diverse: Limarí Chardonnay grown on limestone, Leyda and Casablanca Sauvignon Blanc, Puente Alto Cabernet of real longevity, Carmenère that is finally ripe without being green or jammy, old-vine Carignan from Maule, and País and Cinsault from 100-year-old dry-farmed bush vines in Itata. The Chilean wine map keeps moving south too: a 2025 decree created DOs for the Chiloé archipelago and for Easter Island.

history.title: The vine crosses from Peru
history.text: Spanish conquistadors and missionaries bring Vitis vinifera south from the Viceroyalty of Peru; local tradition credits Francisco de Aguirre with some of the first plantings. The grape is the 'common black grape' later called País, the same Listán Prieto that became Mission in California and Criolla Chica in Argentina.

history.title: País and Moscatel on the dry hills
history.text: Jesuits and settlers spread vineyards through the Central Valley and the south around Concepción and Chillán. Wine for Mass and for the colony is made in clay *tinajas*; sweet wines from País and Moscatel, sometimes boiled to concentrate them, are the colonial style. In 1795 Lima imports 5,000 botijas of wine from Concepción.

history.title: Ochagavía brings Bordeaux to Santiago
history.text: Silvestre Ochagavía Echazarreta imports French vines (Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Malbec, Carmenère and others) and a French winemaker to his estate south of Santiago. The Bordeaux model becomes the template for Chile's elite estates.

history.title: The great Maipo estates
history.text: Cousiño Macul (1856), Errázuriz at Panquehue (1870), Santa Carolina (1875), Santa Rita (1880) and Concha y Toro at Pirque (1883) are founded, mostly by families enriched by silver, copper and banking.

history.title: Phylloxera spares Chile
history.text: As phylloxera devastates European vineyards, Chile's isolation keeps the louse out. French winemakers and vine material arrive, and Chile preserves pre-phylloxera Bordeaux varieties on their own roots, including Carmenère.

history.title: Miguel Torres arrives in Curicó
history.text: The Catalan producer buys land in Curicó and introduces stainless steel tanks and temperature-controlled fermentation, kicking off Chile's technical modernisation.

history.title: Casablanca is planted
history.text: Pablo Morandé plants vines in the Casablanca Valley, opening the first cool coastal region and Chile's white-wine era.

history.title: Decree 464 and the rediscovery of Carmenère
history.text: On 14 December 1994 Decree 464 creates Chile's viticultural zoning of regions, subregions, zones and areas, effective 1995. Weeks earlier, on 24 November, Jean-Michel Boursiquot identifies Carmenère among the 'Merlot' vines at Viña Carmen; SAG recognises the variety officially in 1998.

history.title: Almaviva and the icon era
history.text: Concha y Toro and Baron Philippe de Rothschild launch Almaviva in Puente Alto; Seña (Errázuriz and Mondavi) and Don Melchor complete Chile's first generation of icon wines.

history.title: The Berlin Tasting
history.text: Eduardo Chadwick organises a blind tasting in Berlin where Viñedo Chadwick 2000 and Seña 2001 finish ahead of Lafite, Margaux and Latour.

history.title: Old vines, Costa, Entre Cordilleras, Andes
history.text: The VIGNO association promotes old dry-farmed Maule Carignan; Itata's País and Cinsault are rediscovered; Decree 464 is amended to add the Secano Interior special DO and the Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes label complements.

history.title: Four new DOs
history.text: Apalta, Los Lingues, Licantén and Lo Abarca become DOs, the first defined by vineyard identity rather than municipal boundaries.

history.title: Chiloé and Rapa Nui
history.text: Decree 27, published 14 May 2025, creates a Chiloé subregion and a Rapa Nui-Isla de Pascua area, citing climate change as a reason vines now succeed further south.

history.title: Secano Interior extended, Los Lingues upheld
history.text: Decree 4 (published 14 July 2026) adds seven Biobío communes to the Secano Interior DO; in June the Supreme Court rejects a trademark holder's attempt to annul the Los Lingues DO.

country.classification:
Chile's appellation system is a geographic map with almost no rules about how wine is made, created by Decree 464 of 14 December 1994 (in force from 1995) and administered by the Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero (SAG). It nests four levels: six viticultural Regions (Atacama, Coquimbo, Aconcagua, Valle Central, Sur, Austral), Subregions (mostly the valleys: Elqui, Limarí, Casablanca, Maipo, Rapel, Curicó, Maule, Itata and so on), Zones inside some subregions (Leyda, Cachapoal, Colchagua, Teno, Lontué, Claro, Loncomilla, Tutuvén) and Areas, which usually match one or more communes. Because the units follow municipal lines rather than soil or climate, a single area can stretch from valley floor to Andean summit.

A DO wine must contain at least 75% of grapes from the named place (85% is the norm for export), at least 75% of a named variety and vintage, and up to three regions or subregions can be blended on a label. Approved varieties are listed in the decree, which was widened in 2024 with dozens more. Quality terms (Reserva, Gran Reserva and so on) rest mostly on alcohol above the legal minimum and oak, not on ageing time or yield, so they tell you little.

Three later layers matter more to the wine nerd. Since a 2011 amendment (first used on labels around 2012), wines may add *Costa*, *Entre Cordilleras* or *Andes* if at least 85% of the wine comes from areas declared to have that condition, a much better clue to style than the valley name. The special DO *Secano Interior* (País and Cinsault from dry-farmed land in Maule, Ñuble and Biobío) recognises the old-vine heritage, extended in 2026. And since 2018 small DOs can be drawn around a recognised place or famous vineyard: Apalta, Los Lingues, Licantén and Lo Abarca. Chiloé and Rapa Nui joined in 2025. Producer associations add their own rules, most notably VIGNO for old-vine Maule Carignan.
country.climate_soils:
Almost all of Chile's vineyards sit between 30°S and 38°S, the latitude of North Africa and southern Spain, but the climate is far cooler than that suggests. The Humboldt Current brings Antarctic water up the coast, producing coastal fog (*camanchaca*) and afternoon winds that are channelled inland through gaps in the coastal range. The Andes add nightly katabatic winds and huge day-night swings, while the coastal range shelters the Central Valley and casts a rain shadow. Rainfall rises steeply from north to south: under 100 mm in Elqui and Limarí, about 300 to 350 mm in Maipo, 600 to 700 mm in Colchagua and Maule, over 1,000 mm in Itata and Bío-Bío and around 1,300 mm in Malleco. Summers are dry everywhere, so disease pressure is low, irrigation from Andean snowmelt is usual in the north and centre, and dry farming is possible in the south.

Soils follow the geology of three bands. The coastal range is old granite, weathered into sandy *maicillo* with clay subsoils, with patches of slate (Empedrado), schist and rare limestone (Limarí's Talinay and Quebrada Seca, Lo Abarca). The Central Valley floor is deep alluvium, gravels and clays laid down by Andean rivers such as the Maipo, Cachapoal, Tinguiririca and Maule. The Andean piedmont adds colluvial fans and volcanic material, most famously the stony terraces of Puente Alto. The east-west contrast inside a single valley is often bigger than the north-south one between valleys.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: Chile's most planted grape and its benchmark red; 27.5% of DO wine in 2026. Puente Alto, Pirque and the Andean foothills of Maipo give the classic style of cassis, graphite and a mint or eucalyptus edge.

grapes.name: Carmenère
grapes.note: The lost Bordeaux grape, identified among Chilean 'Merlot' in 1994 and now Chile's signature; best in warm, clay-rich sites such as Peumo, Apalta and Colchagua's valley floor, where it ripens fully and loses its green pepper note. 7.8% of DO wine in 2026.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: Second largest DO volume (17.6% in 2026); the coastal valleys (Casablanca, Leyda, San Antonio, Paredones, Limarí) give a saline, citrus style. Some older Chilean 'Sauvignon' is actually Sauvignonasse (Friulano).

grapes.name: País
grapes.note: Chile's colonial grape (Listán Prieto, Mission, Criolla Chica), planted from the 1550s and still on dry-farmed hills of Maule, Itata and Bío-Bío; reborn as light, earthy reds, rosés and sparkling wines.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: Much of Chile's historic 'Merlot' was Carmenère; true Merlot, planted since the late 1990s, is a major volume grape (12.2% of DO wine in 2026).

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Grown from Limarí to Malleco; the limestone of Limarí and the cool coastal valleys give a tense, mineral style.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.note: Old dry-farmed bush vines in Maule's secano, planted after the 1939 earthquake to add colour and acidity, now championed by VIGNO.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.note: Itata's grape: juicy, light, red-fruited reds from old own-rooted vines on granite.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.note: From warm Colchagua to the cool coast and high Elqui, where it shows pepper and violets.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Coastal sites of Casablanca, Leyda, Limarí and the cool south; increasingly serious.

grapes.name: Moscatel de Alejandría
grapes.note: Old Itata and Bío-Bío vines for dry and orange whites; in Elqui and Limarí a pisco grape.

grapes.name: Malbec (Cot)
grapes.note: Pre-phylloxera Malbec survives in old Maule and Colchagua vineyards; 3% of DO wine.

regions.name: Atacama
regions.tagline: Desert oases of pisco and a few audacious coastal vines.
regions.summary: The northernmost viticultural region, matching the Atacama administrative region, with the Copiapó and Huasco valleys. Almost all of its vineyard serves pisco and table grapes; wine is a curiosity except for coastal experiments in Huasco.
regions.history: Copiapó's wine was a 1950s novelty; Huasco has made sweet *pajarete* since colonial times. Chile's 1931 pisco law already defined Atacama and Coquimbo as the pisco zone.
regions.terroir: Hyper-arid desert with river oases fed by Andean snowmelt; coastal fog makes a few cool sites possible near the sea.
regions.grapes: Moscatel varieties and Pedro Jiménez for pisco; Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah in coastal Huasco.
regions.styles: Pisco above all; small volumes of sweet pajarete and experimental dry wines.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Valle de Copiapó and Valle del Huasco (each = a province).

regions.name: Coquimbo
regions.tagline: Pisco country that learned to make limestone Chardonnay and high-altitude Syrah.
regions.summary: Three transverse valleys, Elqui, Limarí and Choapa, cut across this semi-arid region where Chile narrows between the Andes and the coast. Pisco still takes most of the grapes, but the coastal ends of Limarí and Elqui and the high side valleys of Elqui now produce some of Chile's most distinctive wines.
regions.history: Vines were planted here in the 16th century for wine and aguardiente; pisco became the regional spirit, and the town of La Unión renamed itself Pisco Elqui in 1936. The 1990s brought Falernia in Elqui and Tabalí and Maycas del Limarí in Limarí.
regions.terroir: Desert-edge climate with under 100 mm of rain; Pacific fog and wind near the coast; granite and alluvium, with rare limestone in Limarí's coastal hills; extreme light and cold nights at altitude.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, Pinot Noir; Moscatel and Pedro Jiménez for pisco.
regions.styles: Mineral Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, peppery Syrah, pisco.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Elqui (areas La Serena, Vicuña, Paiguano), Limarí (Ovalle, Monte Patria, Punitaqui, Río Hurtado), Choapa (Salamanca, Illapel).

regions.name: Aconcagua
regions.tagline: Warm Panquehue reds and the cold-coast whites of Casablanca and Leyda.
regions.summary: The Aconcagua viticultural region covers the Valparaíso administrative region. Inland, the Aconcagua Valley gave Chile its first great modern reds; on the coast, Casablanca and San Antonio (Leyda, Lo Abarca) made Chile a white-wine country.
regions.history: Maximiano Errázuriz planted Panquehue in 1870. Casablanca was planted from 1982 by Pablo Morandé; Leyda's vineyards date from 1998 when a pipeline brought Maipo water to the hills; Casa Marín planted Lo Abarca in 2000.
regions.terroir: Warm interior valley with alluvial and colluvial soils; coastal valleys 4 to 30 km from a cold ocean with granite, clay and occasional limestone; frost and water scarcity are the coastal challenges.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Carmenère inland; Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah on the coast.
regions.styles: Ripe Panquehue reds, saline coastal whites, cool-climate Pinot and Syrah.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Aconcagua (nine areas), Casablanca, San Antonio (zone Leyda with San Juan and Santo Domingo; areas Cartagena, Algarrobo; DO Lo Abarca), plus Marga-Marga and the area Zapallar.

regions.name: Valle Central
regions.tagline: Chile's engine room: Maipo Cabernet, Colchagua Carmenère and Maule's old vines.
regions.summary: The Central Valley region runs from the Santiago basin to southern Maule and makes more than four-fifths of Chile's DO wine. Its four subregions (Maipo, Rapel, Curicó, Maule) contain the country's historic estates, its icon Cabernets, its Carmenère heartland and its largest reserve of old dry-farmed vines.
regions.history: From 16th-century País in Maule through the 19th-century Bordeaux estates of Santiago to the export boom of the 1990s, almost every chapter of Chilean wine was written here.
regions.terroir: A tectonic trough between the Andes and coastal range; alluvial valley floors, Andean colluvial terraces and coastal granite; Mediterranean climate with rain rising southwards from about 300 to over 700 mm.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, País, Carignan, Cinsault.
regions.styles: Everything from bulk varietal wine to Chile's most collectable reds.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Maipo, Rapel (zones Cachapoal, Colchagua), Curicó (zones Teno, Lontué), Maule (zones Claro, Loncomilla, Tutuvén) > areas; plus the 2018 DOs Apalta, Los Lingues and Licantén.

regions.name: Valle del Maipo
regions.tagline: The cradle of Chilean Cabernet, from city-edge estates to Puente Alto's stony terraces.
regions.summary: Maipo covers the Metropolitan Region around Santiago. Its Andean sector, Alto Maipo (Puente Alto, Pirque, Santiago), is the source of Chile's most famous Cabernets: Don Melchor, Almaviva, Viñedo Chadwick, Santa Rita's Casa Real and Cousiño Macul.
regions.history: Silvestre Ochagavía's French vines (1851) were planted here, and the great 19th-century estates followed: Cousiño Macul 1856, Santa Carolina 1875, Santa Rita 1880, Concha y Toro 1883. Carmenère was identified at Viña Carmen in Buin in 1994.
regions.terroir: Alluvial cobbles of the Maipo at 600 to 800 m on the Andean side; warmer clay-loams in the centre; coastal granite in the west. About 300 to 350 mm of rain, cold Andean night winds.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon above all, with Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah and Cabernet Franc.
regions.styles: Structured, long-lived Cabernet and Bordeaux blends; ripe Carmenère.
regions.classification: Subregion with thirteen commune-based areas; growers also speak informally of Alto, Central and Pacific Maipo.

regions.name: Valle del Rapel
regions.tagline: Cachapoal and Colchagua: Carmenère's two homes.
regions.summary: Rapel covers the O'Higgins administrative region through its two zones. Cachapoal has Andean Cabernet and the Carmenère of Peumo; Colchagua has the hillside icons of Apalta, the Andean DO Los Lingues and a cool western frontier reaching Paredones.
regions.history: Colonial haciendas such as Los Lingues and El Huique grew wheat and País; the 1990s Apalta projects of Montes and Lapostolle made Colchagua the face of modern Chilean red wine.
regions.terroir: Andean volcanic and colluvial soils in the east, clay alluvium in the centre, granite hills in the west; warm, sunny summers moderated by sea breezes in the west.
regions.grapes: Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Malbec, Merlot, Carignan.
regions.styles: Rich reds; fresher Syrah and whites in the coastal west.
regions.classification: Subregion > zones Cachapoal (six areas) and Colchagua (twelve areas) > 2018 DOs Apalta and Los Lingues.

regions.name: Valle de Curicó
regions.tagline: Where Miguel Torres started Chile's modern era.
regions.summary: Curicó, 200 km south of Santiago, is a varied, productive valley with two zones, Teno and Lontué, plus the coastal DO Licantén.
regions.history: Torres arrived in 1979 with stainless steel; San Pedro at Molina became one of South America's largest vineyards; Valdivieso has made sparkling wine in Lontué since the 19th century.
regions.terroir: Andean piedmont in the east, alluvial valley floor, dry-farmed hills and coastal slate and clay near the Mataquito mouth.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Carmenère, Chardonnay, País.
regions.styles: Reliable varietal wines, sparkling, and old-vine País from the hills.
regions.classification: Subregion > zones Teno (Rauco, Romeral, Vichuquén) and Lontué (Molina, Sagrada Familia); DO Licantén (2018).

regions.name: Valle del Maule
regions.tagline: Chile's biggest vineyard and its deepest reserve of old dry-farmed vines.
regions.summary: Maule produces almost half of Chile's wine and contains three zones: Claro, Loncomilla and Tutuvén (Cauquenes). Beyond its bulk production, it is the home of old-vine Carignan, País and Cinsault on the granite hills of the coastal secano.
regions.history: País was planted here in the 16th century; Carignan was spread after the 1939 Chillán earthquake; VIGNO began codifying Maule Carignan around 2010.
regions.terroir: Volcanic and alluvial soils on the irrigated plain; granite, maicillo and slate on the dry-farmed coastal hills; about 700 mm of rain.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Carmenère, País, Carignan, Cinsault, Malbec.
regions.styles: Bulk varietals; earthy, juicy old-vine reds; increasingly natural-leaning País.
regions.classification: Subregion > zones Claro (six areas), Loncomilla (seven areas), Tutuvén (Cauquenes); much of the secano qualifies for the Secano Interior special DO.

regions.name: Sur
regions.tagline: Old País and Cinsault on granite, and Chardonnay in the rain.
regions.summary: The Southern region combines Itata, Bío-Bío and Malleco. Itata's dry-farmed old vines and Malleco's cool Chardonnay make it the most talked-about part of Chile for adventurous drinkers.
regions.history: The colonial heartland of Chilean wine around Concepción and Chillán; bulk wine through the 20th century; reinvented from the 2010s by small producers and natural winemakers.
regions.terroir: Rolling granite hills (maicillo) near the coast, volcanic soils inland and in Malleco; humid, with over 1,000 mm of rain and a shorter season.
regions.grapes: País, Cinsault, Moscatel de Alejandría, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.styles: Light, fragrant reds; dry and orange Moscatel; taut Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Itata (Chillán, Quillón, Portezuelo, Coelemu), Bío-Bío (Yumbel, Mulchén), Malleco (Traiguén); much of it also Secano Interior.

regions.name: Austral
regions.tagline: The lake district and the islands: Chile's southern frontier.
regions.summary: The Austral region runs from Cautín south to wherever vines will grow. It holds the Cautín and Osorno valleys and, since 2025, the Chiloé archipelago.
regions.history: Defined in 1994 with an open southern limit; Casa Silva's Lago Ranco vineyard showed the potential; Chiloé added by Decree 27 (published May 2025).
regions.terroir: Cool, wet temperate climate; volcanic soils; short growing season.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling.
regions.styles: Sparkling and high-acid whites, light Pinot Noir.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Valle del Cautín, Valle de Osorno, Chiloé.
