cl-aconcagua.name: Aconcagua
cl-aconcagua.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon
cl-aconcagua.nerd_note: Zapallar and the Marga-Marga valley sit directly under the region in the decree's table, outside any subregion.
cl-aconcagua.summary: The viticultural region that matches the Valparaíso administrative region. It is named after the Aconcagua river and mountain (6,961 m, the highest peak outside Asia), but its modern fame rests as much on the cool coastal valleys of Casablanca and San Antonio as on the warm inland Aconcagua Valley itself. SAG's 2024 census put its wine vineyard at about 7,760 ha, roughly two-thirds white varieties, which tells you how the coast has reshaped it.

cl-algarrobo.name: Algarrobo
cl-algarrobo.summary: Area matching Algarrobo commune on the northern coast of San Antonio province, a beach-resort town with a few cool vineyards in the hills behind it. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-alhue.name: Alhué
cl-alhue.summary: Area matching Alhué commune, a secluded valley in the coastal range at the south-western edge of the Metropolitan Region, with a few vineyards among old haciendas. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-apalta.name: Apalta
cl-apalta.grapes: Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Merlot, Malbec, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan
cl-apalta.terroir: Decomposed granite on steep slopes, deeper alluvial clay on the horseshoe floor; south-facing amphitheatre with shortened direct sun hours and morning mist.
cl-apalta.nerd_note: Montes Folly was the first Syrah planted on Apalta's steepest slopes in the 1990s; locals thought it mad, hence the name.
cl-apalta.summary:
Apalta is the most famous hillside in Chile: a horseshoe of granite slopes opening south onto the Tinguiririca river near Santa Cruz in Colchagua, recognised as its own DO in 2018 with about 1,007 ha of vineyards. The hills shelter it on three sides, so morning mist lingers and direct sun arrives late and leaves early, slowing ripening in what would otherwise be a hot valley. Valley floor clay suits Cabernet and Carmenère; the poorer granitic slopes, terraced since the 1990s, increasingly carry Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre and Carignan.

The names are legendary: Lapostolle's Clos Apalta, a Carmenère-led blend from vines planted in the early 20th century, made in a gravity winery dug into the hill; Montes Alpha M and the steep Syrah of Montes Folly; and Neyen, an old adobe estate with Carmenère and Cabernet over a century old. Apalta wines are dense and dark but carry a fresh, granite-edged finish. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-atacama.name: Atacama
cl-atacama.grapes: Moscatel varieties and Pedro Jiménez (mostly for pisco); Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah
cl-atacama.nerd_note: Huasco's traditional sweet *pajarete*, a cooked-must style from the upper valley around Alto del Carmen, is one of the oldest wine styles still made in Chile.
cl-atacama.summary: The northernmost of Chile's six viticultural regions, matching the administrative Región de Atacama and split into the Copiapó and Huasco valleys. This is pisco country first and wine country a distant second: SAG's 2024 census counted about 560 ha of pisco grapes against under 60 ha of wine grapes. What wine there is comes from desert river oases fed by Andean snowmelt, plus a few daring coastal plantings in Huasco where the Pacific fog makes cool-climate Chardonnay and Pinot Noir possible at latitude 28°S.

cl-austral.name: Austral
cl-austral.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Gewürztraminer
cl-austral.nerd_note: The only Chilean region whose southern limit is not a line on a map but a viticultural condition written into the decree.
cl-austral.summary: Chile's southernmost viticultural region, defined in 1994 as running from Cautín province 'as far south as soil and climate allow the vine to grow'. It began with the Cautín and Osorno valleys; in 2025 a decree added the Chiloé archipelago as a third subregion, explicitly justified by climate change pushing viable viticulture south. Vineyards are tiny (a few dozen hectares across Araucanía, Los Ríos and Los Lagos in 2024) and focus on Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling with high natural acidity.

cl-buin.name: Buin
cl-buin.summary: Area defined by Buin, Paine and San Bernardo communes, the Central Maipo heartland south of Santiago. It includes Alto Jahuel, home of Santa Rita (founded 1880), and Viña Carmen, where in 1994 Jean-Michel Boursiquot identified Carmenère among the vines Chileans called Merlot. Warm days and alluvial soils give rich Cabernet and Carmenère. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-calera-de-tango.name: Calera de Tango
cl-calera-de-tango.summary: Area matching Calera de Tango commune, a small farming district south-west of Santiago with some Cabernet and other reds. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-calle-larga.name: Calle Larga
cl-calle-larga.summary: Area matching Calle Larga commune near Los Andes, on the Andean piedmont where stony soils and mountain breezes shape fresher reds. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-cartagena.name: Cartagena
cl-cartagena.summary: Area matching Cartagena commune on the San Antonio coast. It includes the village of Lo Abarca (which became its own DO in 2018) and Matetic's Rosario valley vineyards, a few kilometres inland. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-catemu.name: Catemu
cl-catemu.summary: Area matching Catemu commune, a warm side basin of the Aconcagua valley with mixed fruit farming and some vineyards for red varieties. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-cauquenes.name: Cauquenes
cl-cauquenes.nerd_note: The Lomas de Cauquenes cooperative still crushes grapes from hundreds of small dry-farm growers.
cl-cauquenes.summary: Cauquenes is the epicentre of Chile's rediscovered heritage. On the granite hills of the coastal range, bush-trained, dry-farmed País and Carignan up to 100 to 200 years old grow without irrigation, ploughed by horse, picked into wooden boxes. For decades the grapes went to cheap *pipeño* and jug wine; since the late 2000s VIGNO Carignan, Miguel Torres's sparkling País (Estelado) and a crowd of small natural-leaning producers have turned the commune into a source of juicy, earthy, low-alcohol reds. It is the single area of the Valle del Tutuvén zone and part of the Secano Interior. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-chillan.name: Chillán
cl-chillan.summary: Area defined by Chillán, Bulnes, San Carlos, Chillán Viejo and Ñiquén communes, the inland Itata around the capital of Ñuble. Valley-floor vineyards and some old País and Moscatel on the surrounding hills. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-chiloe.name: Chiloé
cl-chiloe.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling
cl-chiloe.nerd_note: The same 2025 decree created a DO for Rapa Nui (Easter Island), 3,700 km out in the Pacific.
cl-chiloe.summary: Chiloé became a Chilean DO subregion in 2025: Decree 27 of November 2024, published on 14 May 2025, added the whole archipelago of Chiloé province to the Austral region. The decree's own reasoning is striking: climate change has widened the latitude where vines can grow, and the islands' insular conditions now produce distinctive quality wine. Plantings near 42°S are minuscule, mainly cool-climate whites and Pinot Noir, and the DO is one of the southernmost legally defined wine areas anywhere, though Argentina's Chubut IGs reach further south.

cl-chimbarongo.name: Chimbarongo
cl-chimbarongo.summary: Area matching Chimbarongo commune in east Colchagua, known for wicker crafts as well as vineyards on the Andean side of the valley. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-coelemu.name: Coelemu
cl-coelemu.summary: Area defined by Coelemu and Treguaco communes near the mouth of the Itata. It includes Guarilihue, the granite hamlet where De Martino and others source century-old Cinsault and Moscatel for wines fermented in clay *tinajas*. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-colbun.name: Colbún
cl-colbun.summary: Area matching Colbún commune on the Andean side of Maule, near the Colbún reservoir; piedmont vineyards give fresher reds. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-colina.name: Colina
cl-colina.summary: Area matching Colina commune north of Santiago, Chacabuco province. Vineyards are few and squeezed by suburban growth. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-coltauco.name: Coltauco
cl-coltauco.summary: Area matching Coltauco commune in west Cachapoal, a mixed farming district with some red plantings. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-coquimbo.name: Coquimbo
cl-coquimbo.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, Pinot Noir; Pedro Jiménez and Moscatel for pisco
cl-coquimbo.nerd_note: The region produced 58 million litres of DO wine in 2026, 7.4% of Chile's DO total, a share far larger than its reputation as 'pisco country' suggests.
cl-coquimbo.summary: Chile's second viticultural region from the north, matching the Coquimbo administrative region and its three transverse valleys, Elqui, Limarí and Choapa. Here the Atacama Desert gives way to semi-arid scrub; the country narrows to under 200 km and the Andes and the coastal range nearly touch. Pisco still dominates the vineyard (about 8,700 ha of pisco grapes in 2024), but since the 1990s the region has become the source of some of Chile's most distinctive wines: chalk-influenced Chardonnay from Limarí's coastal hills and peppery high-altitude Syrah from Elqui.

cl-curepto.name: Curepto
cl-curepto.summary: Area matching Curepto commune near the Mataquito mouth, in the coastal secano, with old dry-farmed País and newer coastal plantings. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-empedrado.name: Empedrado
cl-empedrado.summary: Area matching Empedrado commune in Maule's coastal range, one of the few slate terroirs in Chile. Miguel Torres planted a vineyard on its schist slopes in the 2000s, producing a rare, mineral Pinot Noir. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-hijuelas.name: Hijuelas
cl-hijuelas.summary: Area matching Hijuelas commune between Quillota and Llaillay. It includes the Ocoa hills where Seña planted its biodynamic hillside vineyard in 1998, after the wine's early vintages were sourced from Panquehue. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-illapel.name: Illapel
cl-illapel.summary: Area matching Illapel commune in the Choapa valley, around the provincial capital. Vineyards are scattered and small, part of a mixed farming landscape of table grapes and fruit. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-isla-de-maipo.name: Isla de Maipo
cl-isla-de-maipo.summary: Area matching Isla de Maipo commune, an island-like tract between arms of the Maipo river in central Maipo. De Martino and Tarapacá are based here; the warm, alluvial valley floor produces ripe Cabernet, Carmenère and Syrah. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-la-estrella.name: La Estrella
cl-la-estrella.summary: Area matching La Estrella commune in the western hills of Colchagua, with granitic soils and limited, recent plantings. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-la-serena.name: La Serena
cl-la-serena.summary: Area matching La Serena commune at the mouth of the Elqui, the valley's coastal end. Morning fog and sea breezes make it the coolest part of Elqui, suited to Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay, though vineyards are scattered among the city's sprawl and farms. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-lampa.name: Lampa
cl-lampa.summary: Area matching Lampa commune north-west of Santiago; minor vineyard area in a rapidly urbanising basin. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-licanten.name: Licantén
cl-licanten.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Carmenère
cl-licanten.summary: Licantén is a small coastal DO of about 124 ha in the Mataquito valley of Curicó, created in 2018. Its only producer, La Ronciere, planted the Idahue vineyard in 2012 about 24 km from the sea, entirely to red varieties, on four soil types including llicorella-like slate, lutites, gravel and clay. Cool Pacific air gives Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Carmenère a fresher, more tensile profile than the inland Curicó style. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-linares.name: Linares
cl-linares.summary: Area defined by Linares and Yerbas Buenas communes, a large valley-floor vineyard zone with some old vines in the surrounding hills. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-litueche.name: Litueche
cl-litueche.summary: Area matching Litueche commune in Cardenal Caro province near the coast, a cool frontier with a handful of vineyards. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-llay-llay.name: Llaillay
cl-llay-llay.summary: Area matching Llaillay commune (Llay-Llay on many maps), a windy gap where the Aconcagua valley narrows; vineyards here are few and mostly red. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-lo-abarca.name: Lo Abarca
cl-lo-abarca.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir, Syrah
cl-lo-abarca.nerd_note: Casa Marín's single-vineyard names (Cipreses, Laurel, Miramar) map individual slopes of this one hillside DO.
cl-lo-abarca.summary: Lo Abarca is Chile's tiniest DO, about 44.5 ha around a hamlet 4 km from the Pacific in the San Antonio Valley, and in practice it is one producer's vineyard: Casa Marín, planted from 2000 by María Luz Marín against every adviser's warning. Created by decree in 2018 (one of the first DOs not tied to a commune), it has calcareous and granitic slopes, cold fog and wind, and produces Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir and Syrah of startling salinity. Labels carry the complement *Costa*.

cl-lolol.name: Lolol
cl-lolol.summary: Area matching Lolol commune in west Colchagua, a valley of old adobe houses and newer hillside vineyards where coastal influence cools Syrah, Cabernet and Rhône varieties. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-longavi.name: Longaví
cl-longavi.summary: Area matching Longaví commune in southern Maule. The brand Longaví, from the Garcés Silva family's young winemakers, takes its name from the volcano. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-los-lingues.name: Los Lingues
cl-los-lingues.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
cl-los-lingues.nerd_note: Koyle, founded by members of the Undurraga family, has about 80 ha planted inside the DO.
cl-los-lingues.summary: Los Lingues is a 492 ha Andes-side DO in San Fernando commune, east Colchagua, created by Supreme Decree 56 of 2017 and published in 2018. It takes its name from the colonial Hacienda Los Lingues, one of the oldest estates in Chile, and its vineyards (Koyle, Casa Silva, Siegel) sit on volcanic and colluvial soils with basalt rocks at the foot of the cordillera, where cool mountain breezes give firmer, fresher Cabernet, Carmenère and Syrah than the warm valley floor. In June 2026 Chile's Supreme Court upheld the DO against a trademark holder who had registered 'Los Lingues' brands since 1983, confirming that a denomination of origin can coexist with an earlier trademark. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-machali.name: Machalí
cl-machali.summary: Area matching Machalí commune, a large Andean commune east of Rancagua reaching into the high cordillera; its vineyards sit on the piedmont near the Cachapoal canyon. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-marchigue.name: Marchigüe
cl-marchigue.summary: Area matching Marchigüe commune, the west Colchagua frontier planted from the late 1990s, notably by Montes and Montgras. Rolling granite hills, a breeze from the Pacific and low rainfall give Syrah, Cabernet and Carmenère with freshness and grip. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-maria-pinto.name: María Pinto
cl-maria-pinto.summary: Area matching María Pinto commune, in the hills west of Santiago between Curacaví and Melipilla, a minor source of red grapes. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-melipilla.name: Melipilla
cl-melipilla.summary: Area defined by Melipilla and San Pedro communes, the western 'Pacific Maipo' sector, where sea breezes reach through the coastal range. Newer plantings of Cabernet, Syrah and some whites experiment with this cooler fringe. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-molina.name: Molina
cl-molina.summary: Area defined by Molina, Río Claro and Curicó communes. It holds San Pedro's vast estate at Lontué and Miguel Torres's winery near Curicó, where Torres began modernising Chilean winemaking in 1979. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-monte-patria.name: Monte Patria
cl-monte-patria.summary: Area matching Monte Patria commune in the upper Limarí basin, where the Grande and Huatulame rivers come down from the Andes. Warm, dry and high, it grows mainly pisco and table grapes, with some Syrah and Cabernet for wine. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-mulchen.name: Mulchén
cl-mulchen.summary: Area defined by Mulchén, Nacimiento and Negrete communes, cool and rainy, planted to Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and aromatic whites. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-nancagua.name: Nancagua
cl-nancagua.summary: Area defined by Nancagua and Placilla communes on the Colchagua valley floor, warm alluvial land with large vineyards of Cabernet, Carmenère and Merlot. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-ovalle.name: Ovalle
cl-ovalle.summary: Area matching Ovalle commune, the lower Limarí valley that includes the limestone hills of Talinay and Quebrada Seca near the coast. This is where Limarí's reputation for mineral Chardonnay and Pinot Noir is made, by Tabalí, Concha y Toro and others. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-paiguano.name: Paiguano
cl-paiguano.nerd_note: The decree spells it Paiguano; road signs and most maps say Paihuano.
cl-paiguano.summary: Area matching Paiguano commune (also spelled Paihuano), the upper Elqui where the Claro river valley climbs past Pisco Elqui towards Alcohuaz. Small terraced vineyards at 1,500 to around 2,000 m give some of the highest-altitude wines in Chile, mostly Syrah, Garnacha, Carignan and Malbec, alongside traditional pisco grapes. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-palmilla.name: Palmilla
cl-palmilla.summary: Area matching Palmilla commune in central Colchagua, which includes the colonial Hacienda El Huique; Montgras and others farm warm valley vineyards nearby. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-panquehue.name: Panquehue
cl-panquehue.summary: Area matching Panquehue commune, the warm heart of the inland Aconcagua valley and home of Viña Errázuriz since 1870, with its Max Viñedo hillside vineyard and the Don Maximiano estate. Long, hot summer afternoons give ripe, structured Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Carmenère. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-paredones.name: Paredones
cl-paredones.summary: Area matching Paredones commune, Colchagua's coastal end about 10 to 15 km from the Pacific. Casa Silva and others planted here in the 2000s and showed that the warm-red zone of Colchagua can also make saline Sauvignon Blanc and taut Pinot Noir on granite and schist. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-parral.name: Parral
cl-parral.summary: Area matching Parral commune, birthplace of Pablo Neruda, in southern Maule; mixed irrigated and dry-farmed vineyards. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-pencahue.name: Pencahue
cl-pencahue.summary: Area matching Pencahue commune west of Talca, warm and relatively dry, known for ripe reds and dry-farmed old vines. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-peralillo.name: Peralillo
cl-peralillo.summary: Area matching Peralillo commune, home of Los Vascos, the estate bought in 1988 by Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite), one of the first foreign investments of Chile's modern wine boom. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-peumo.name: Peumo
cl-peumo.nerd_note: Before Boursiquot's 1994 identification, Chilean growers called this vine 'Merlot Peumal', after Peumo.
cl-peumo.summary: Area defined by Peumo, Pichidegua, Las Cabras and San Vicente communes in west Cachapoal: Chile's Carmenère grand cru in all but name. Clay-rich alluvial soils near the Cachapoal river, a warm sheltered bowl and a long autumn let the late-ripening grape lose its green pyrazines. Concha y Toro's Carmín de Peumo and Terrunyo Carmenère come from its Peumo vineyard; Vik sits in the Millahue valley of San Vicente. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-pirque.name: Pirque
cl-pirque.summary: Area matching Pirque commune, on the south bank of the Maipo where the river leaves the Andes. Concha y Toro founded its winery here in 1883 at the Subercaseaux family's country house, and the commune also holds Haras de Pirque (a horse-stud estate turned winery) and William Fèvre Chile. Cold air pouring out of the Maipo canyon at night keeps Cabernet fresh and structured. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-portezuelo.name: Portezuelo
cl-portezuelo.summary: Area defined by Portezuelo, Ninhue, Quirihue and San Nicolás communes, the north-western coastal hills of Itata with some of its oldest dry-farmed País and Cinsault. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-puente-alto.name: Puente Alto
cl-puente-alto.nerd_note: Viñedo Chadwick was a polo field until Eduardo Chadwick planted it in 1992 at his family's Puente Alto property.
cl-puente-alto.summary: Area matching Puente Alto and La Pintana communes on the north bank of the Maipo: the most valuable Cabernet terroir in Chile. On a stony alluvial terrace at about 650 m sit Concha y Toro's Don Melchor vineyard, Almaviva and Viñedo Chadwick, side by side. Deep, free-draining river cobbles, cool mountain nights and a long dry season give Cabernet of fine tannin, cassis and graphite that ages for decades. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-pumanque.name: Pumanque
cl-pumanque.summary: Area matching Pumanque commune in the west of Colchagua, a rural district of old haciendas with small coastal-influenced plantings. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-punitaqui.name: Punitaqui
cl-punitaqui.summary: Area matching Punitaqui commune, a small inland basin south of Ovalle between the coastal and Andean ranges. Vineyards are few and mostly for pisco and bulk wine. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-quillon.name: Quillón
cl-quillon.summary: Area defined by Quillón, Ránquil and Florida communes in southern Itata, where the Itata river runs between granite hills dotted with old Moscatel and Cinsault. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-quillota.name: Quillota
cl-quillota.summary: Area matching Quillota commune in the lower Aconcagua valley, famous for avocados and cherimoyas. Its vineyards benefit from the coastal influence and suit Syrah and cooler-climate reds. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-rancagua.name: Rancagua
cl-rancagua.summary: Area defined by Rancagua, Graneros, Mostazal, Codegua and Olivar communes around the O'Higgins capital, the northern gateway of Cachapoal, with mixed red plantings. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-rapa-nui-isla-de-pascua.name: Rapa Nui - Isla de Pascua
cl-rapa-nui-isla-de-pascua.nerd_note: Rapa Nui is the only Chilean DO not attached to any viticultural region or subregion.
cl-rapa-nui-isla-de-pascua.summary: Almost certainly the most remote wine appellation in the world: Easter Island, about 3,700 km off the Chilean coast in the South Pacific, became a Chilean DO area through Decree 27 (signed November 2024, published May 2025). It covers the island's entire commune and sits outside every viticultural region, listed on its own as numeral 7 of article 1. The government's stated aim was to give the island's handful of subtropical vineyards the same labelling rights as mainland wine; volumes are tiny and the subtropical, humid climate makes any wine here an experiment.

cl-rauco.name: Rauco
cl-rauco.summary: Area defined by Rauco and Hualañé communes, west of Curicó city, with dry-farmed hills that qualify for the Secano Interior special DO for País and Cinsault. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-rengo.name: Rengo
cl-rengo.summary: Area defined by Rengo, Malloa and Quinta de Tilcoco communes in central Cachapoal, with Torreón de Paredes and Misiones de Rengo among its wineries. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-requinoa.name: Requínoa
cl-requinoa.summary: Area matching Requínoa commune at the foot of the Andes in east Cachapoal. Altaïr, the San Pedro project created with Château Dassault in the early 2000s, and other Andes-side estates grow structured Cabernet blends on stony colluvial slopes. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-retiro.name: Retiro
cl-retiro.summary: Area matching Retiro commune in southern Maule, irrigated farmland with vineyards for Cabernet and País. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-rio-hurtado.name: Río Hurtado
cl-rio-hurtado.summary: Area matching Río Hurtado commune, a narrow Andean side valley of the Limarí known for dark skies and small fruit farms. Its few vineyards serve pisco and local wine. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-romeral.name: Romeral
cl-romeral.summary: Area defined by Romeral and Teno communes, the Andes side of Curicó, where cool mountain breezes favour Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-sagrada-familia.name: Sagrada Familia
cl-sagrada-familia.summary: Area matching Sagrada Familia commune, south-west of Curicó, where valley floor gives way to dry-farmed hills with old País; part of the Secano Interior. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-salamanca.name: Salamanca
cl-salamanca.summary: Area matching Salamanca commune in the upper Choapa valley, an Andean foothill zone of stony soils and mining country. Syrah and Cabernet from here go mostly to wineries outside the valley. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-san-clemente.name: San Clemente
cl-san-clemente.summary: Area matching San Clemente commune, a huge Andean commune east of Talca stretching to the Argentine border; vineyards on the piedmont give fresh Cabernet and Sauvignon Blanc. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-san-esteban.name: San Esteban
cl-san-esteban.summary: Area matching San Esteban commune, the highest part of the Aconcagua valley. Viña San Esteban's In Situ project farms here, beside petroglyph-covered rocks of Paidahuen hill that recall the valley's pre-Hispanic people. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-san-felipe.name: San Felipe
cl-san-felipe.summary: Area matching San Felipe commune, the provincial capital of the upper Aconcagua valley, warm and irrigated, with plantings of Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah among fruit orchards. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-san-fernando.name: San Fernando
cl-san-fernando.summary: Area matching San Fernando commune, the eastern, Andes-side gateway to Colchagua. It contains the historic Hacienda Los Lingues (now its own DO), Casa Silva's Angostura winery and cool piedmont vineyards whose volcanic soils give firmer, fresher reds. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-san-javier.name: San Javier
cl-san-javier.summary: Area matching San Javier commune, the hub of Maule's old-vine revival. Gillmore at Villavicencio and the Bouchon family at Mingre farm dry-farmed Carignan, País and Cabernet in the coastal hills, and many VIGNO Carignans come from here. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-san-juan.name: San Juan
cl-san-juan.summary: Area of the Valle de Leyda zone defined by San Antonio commune, covering much of the Leyda hills around the village of Leyda itself. Viña Leyda and Amayna farm here on granite with clay, a few kilometres from the sea. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-san-rafael.name: San Rafael
cl-san-rafael.summary: Area matching San Rafael commune north of Talca (not to be confused with Argentina's San Rafael DOC), a farming district with red plantings. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-santa-cruz.name: Santa Cruz
cl-santa-cruz.summary: Area defined by Santa Cruz and Chépica communes, the tourist heart of Colchagua. It includes the Apalta horseshoe (now its own DO) and the town's Colchagua Museum; valley-floor vineyards here give generous Carmenère and Cabernet. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-santa-maria.name: Santa María
cl-santa-maria.summary: Area matching Santa María commune in the upper Aconcagua, at the foot of the Andes. Cool mountain air at night helps reds keep freshness. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-santiago.name: Santiago
cl-santiago.summary: Area defined in the decree by the communes of Peñalolén and La Florida, on Santiago's eastern edge. It holds the last city-fringe vineyards of the 19th-century estates: Cousiño Macul's original Macul vineyard (founded 1856, now much reduced by housing) and Viña Aquitania, founded in 1990 by Bruno Prats and Paul Pontallier of Bordeaux. Alluvial gravels under the Andes give firm, classic Cabernet. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-santo-domingo.name: Santo Domingo
cl-santo-domingo.summary: Area of the Valle de Leyda zone defined by Santo Domingo commune, south of the port of San Antonio near the Maipo river mouth. Coastal vineyards here are among the coolest in the zone. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-secano-interior.name: Secano Interior
cl-secano-interior.nerd_note: The decree formally recognises Mission and Criolla as accepted synonyms of País, linking Chile's grape to California's Mission and Argentina's Criolla Chica (all Listán Prieto).
cl-secano-interior.summary:
Secano Interior ('dry interior') is a special denomination of origin for wines made only from País and Cinsault grown on unirrigated land in the coastal hills and interior of Maule, Ñuble and Biobío. It rescues a category the 1994 law had effectively excluded: País was not even on the list of varieties allowed for DO wine. The decree names the qualifying areas (Rauco, Romeral, Molina, Sagrada Familia, Talca, Pencahue, San Clemente, San Rafael, San Javier, Villa Alegre, Parral, Linares, Cauquenes, Chillán, Quillón, Portezuelo, Coelemu and Yumbel) plus further communes; in July 2026 Decree 4 added Hualqui, Nacimiento, Los Ángeles, Laja, San Rosendo, Santa Juana and Tomé in Biobío.

The label can read 'Secano Interior' followed by the subregion, zone or area. SAG recorded 5.4 million litres under this DO in 2026, small but symbolic: it gives legal standing to the dry-farmed, own-rooted, often centenarian bush vines that are now Chile's hottest wine story.

cl-sur.name: Sur
cl-sur.grapes: País, Cinsault, Moscatel de Alejandría, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling
cl-sur.nerd_note: SAG counted 10,323 ha of wine grapes in Ñuble alone in 2024, more than the entire Metropolitan Region that holds the Maipo.
cl-sur.summary: The Southern region (Región del Sur) runs from the Ñuble river country to Malleco in Araucanía and contains the Itata, Bío-Bío and Malleco valleys. It is where Chile's colonial viticulture survived most intact: dry-farmed, head-trained País, Cinsault and Moscatel on granite hills that never saw the 1980s modernisation. Rainfall is higher (often over 1,000 mm), summers shorter, and the new wave of growers has turned it into the most exciting source of old-vine and cool-climate wine in the country.

cl-talagante.name: Talagante
cl-talagante.summary: Area defined by Talagante, Peñaflor, El Monte and Padre Hurtado communes, west of Santiago. Undurraga, founded here in 1885 by Francisco Undurraga, still has its historic winery and park at Santa Ana. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-talca.name: Talca
cl-talca.summary: Area defined by Talca, Maule and Pelarco communes around Maule's capital, with irrigated valley vineyards and dry-farmed hills that qualify for Secano Interior. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-til-til.name: Til Til
cl-til-til.summary: Area matching Til Til commune in the far north of the Metropolitan Region, a dry, warm basin with scattered vineyards. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-traiguen.name: Traiguén
cl-traiguen.summary: Area matching Traiguén commune in Malleco, where Viña Aquitania planted the Sol de Sol Chardonnay vineyard in the 1990s and Baettig and others have followed with taut Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-valle-central.name: Valle Central
cl-valle-central.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, País, Carignan
cl-valle-central.nerd_note: 'Valle Central' on a label is often a blend across all four subregions, the Chilean equivalent of a regional entry-level wine.
cl-valle-central.summary: The Central Valley region is the engine of Chilean wine: the long tectonic trough between the Andes and the coastal range from Santiago's Chacabuco province south to Cauquenes and Linares in Maule. It holds four subregions (Maipo, Rapel, Curicó, Maule) and, by SAG's figures, made 661.6 million litres of DO wine in 2026, 83.7% of the national total. The name covers everything from Puente Alto's Cabernet terraces to 19th-century País vines on the Maule dry-farmed hills, so on a serious bottle you will almost always see a subregion, zone or area instead.

cl-valle-de-casablanca.name: Valle de Casablanca
cl-valle-de-casablanca.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah, Gewürztraminer
cl-valle-de-casablanca.terroir: Granitic hills with clay-loam and sandy topsoils on the valley floor; marine fog and afternoon winds; frequent spring frost; no river irrigation, so wells and reservoirs.
cl-valle-de-casablanca.nerd_note: Casablanca is the exception to Chile's ungrafted-vine story: nematodes in its sandy soils make rootstocks a sensible choice here.
cl-valle-de-casablanca.summary:
Casablanca turned Chile into a white-wine country. In 1982 Pablo Morandé planted vines in this flat, frost-prone valley halfway between Santiago and Valparaíso, against the advice of almost everyone, because the Pacific 20 to 30 km away pushes cold fog and wind through gaps in the coastal range every afternoon. The result was the first truly cool-climate wine region in a country that had only known the warm Central Valley: crisp Sauvignon Blanc, citrus-and-butter Chardonnay and, as growers moved up the slopes, Pinot Noir and cool Syrah.

The valley rises gently from about 200 m in the east to 400 m near the coast, and the western end (Lo Ovalle, Las Dichas, Tapihue) is markedly cooler than the eastern Lo Vásquez end along Ruta 68. Spring frost is the great hazard, and water is scarce: there is no Andean river, so growers rely on wells and reservoirs. Casablanca is also one of the few Chilean regions where grafting is common, because its sandy soils host nematodes.

In the glass, good Casablanca Sauvignon shows grapefruit, herbs and a salty finish; Chardonnay is fresher than Central Valley versions; Pinot Noir and Syrah from Matetic-style slopes are peppery and red-fruited. The entire commune is one subregion with no internal areas, and labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-valle-de-colchagua.name: Valle de Colchagua
cl-valle-de-colchagua.grapes: Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Malbec, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Carignan; Sauvignon Blanc near the coast
cl-valle-de-colchagua.terroir: Clay-loam and alluvium on the valley floor, decomposed granite on the hillsides (Apalta, Marchigüe), volcanic soils towards the Andes; Mediterranean climate with about 600 mm of rain, warm days and cooler coastal west.
cl-valle-de-colchagua.summary:
Colchagua is Chile's red-wine showcase, the southern zone of Rapel running from the Andes past San Fernando and Santa Cruz to the Pacific at Pichilemu along the Tinguiririca river. Its colonial haciendas (Los Lingues, Huique) grew País and wheat for centuries; the transformation began in the 1990s, when Aurelio Montes, Alexandra Marnier-Lapostolle and others bet on the granite hillsides of Apalta, and Robert Parker's praise for Montes Alpha M and Clos Apalta made the valley a brand. Santa Cruz grew into Chile's wine-tourism capital, with its Colchagua Museum and wine train.

The zone splits three ways. The eastern Andes side (San Fernando, Chimbarongo, Los Lingues) is cooler, with volcanic and colluvial soils. The centre (Nancagua, Santa Cruz, Palmilla, Peralillo and the Apalta horseshoe) is warm and sunny, the classic home of rich Carmenère, Cabernet, Syrah and Malbec. The west (Marchigüe, Lolol, Pumanque, Paredones, La Estrella, Litueche) is the 2000s frontier, where coastal breezes and granite give fresher Syrah, Cabernet and even Sauvignon Blanc at Paredones, 10 km from the sea.

Colchagua's house style is generous: ripe black fruit, soft tannins, sweet spice. The best hillside wines balance that sunshine with granite-born freshness.

cl-valle-de-copiapo.name: Valle de Copiapó
cl-valle-de-copiapo.summary: Subregion matching Copiapó province, a desert river oasis at about 27°S where table grapes and pisco grapes vastly outnumber wine vines. Wine production here was a 1950s novelty around the city of Copiapó and remains marginal; the valley matters to the atlas as the northern edge of Chile's DO system.

cl-valle-de-curico.name: Valle de Curicó
cl-valle-de-curico.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Carmenère, Chardonnay, País
cl-valle-de-curico.nerd_note: Valdivieso, based in Lontué, has made traditional-method sparkling wine since the 1880s, among the oldest in South America.
cl-valle-de-curico.summary:
Curicó, about 200 km south of Santiago, is where Chile's modern wine era began. In 1979 the Catalan producer Miguel Torres bought land here and brought stainless steel tanks and temperature-controlled fermentation, technologies that spread through the country in the following decade. The subregion covers Curicó province plus Río Claro commune and has two zones: Teno in the north and Lontué in the south.

It is a workhorse valley with more grape varieties than anywhere else in Chile, best known for reliable Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc, and home to big producers such as San Pedro at Molina, whose vineyard is among the largest single blocks in South America. Its edges are where the action is now: the dry-farmed hills of Rauco and Sagrada Familia (part of the Secano Interior), and the coastal Licantén DO near the mouth of the Mataquito.

cl-valle-de-leyda.name: Valle de Leyda
cl-valle-de-leyda.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Syrah
cl-valle-de-leyda.summary: Leyda is a zone of the San Antonio Valley, made of the San Juan (San Antonio commune) and Santo Domingo areas, and the name most cool-climate fans know. Its gently rolling hills sit 8 to 15 km from the Pacific; the decisive moment came in 1998 when the Fernández family ran an 8 km pipeline from the Maipo to irrigate Viña Leyda. Today Leyda Sauvignon Blanc is a benchmark of saline, citrus-driven Chilean white, with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay close behind.

cl-valle-de-osorno.name: Valle de Osorno
cl-valle-de-osorno.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling
cl-valle-de-osorno.summary: Osorno covers Osorno, San Pablo and Purranque communes in Los Lagos plus La Unión and Futrono in Los Ríos, near 40°S. Casa Silva's vineyard on the shores of Lake Ranco at Futrono, planted in the 2000s, makes sparkling wine, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir with piercing acidity, proving that the lake district can ripen grapes in warm years.

cl-valle-de-san-antonio.name: Valle de San Antonio
cl-valle-de-san-antonio.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah
cl-valle-de-san-antonio.terroir: Granite and decomposed granite with clay topsoils, calcareous patches at Lo Abarca; 4 to 15 km from the Pacific; morning fog, cold breezes, low rainfall and water scarcity.
cl-valle-de-san-antonio.nerd_note: Matetic's estate straddles the border with Casablanca, and its Rosario valley vineyards sit in San Antonio's Cartagena area.
cl-valle-de-san-antonio.summary:
The San Antonio Valley, matching San Antonio province on the coast west of Santiago, is the sharpest of Chile's cool-climate frontiers. The first vines went in only in the late 1990s and 2000: Viña Leyda's founders piped water 8 km from the Maipo river to plant the Leyda hills in 1998, and María Luz Marín planted her vineyard at Lo Abarca, 4 km from the sea, in 2000. Cold Humboldt Current water offshore keeps summers cool, and sites sit 4 to 15 km from the Pacific on granitic hills, some with a cap of clay and patches of limestone.

The wines are thrillingly tense: Sauvignon Blanc with crushed-rock salinity and passion fruit, Chardonnay with high acidity, savoury Pinot Noir and some of Chile's most peppery Syrah. The subregion contains the Valle de Leyda zone (San Juan and Santo Domingo areas), the areas of Cartagena and Algarrobo, and since 2018 the tiny Lo Abarca DO. Labels from all of it may carry the complement *Costa*.

cl-valle-del-aconcagua.name: Valle del Aconcagua
cl-valle-del-aconcagua.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Syrah, Merlot; Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir near the coast
cl-valle-del-aconcagua.terroir: Alluvial and colluvial soils on the warm valley floor at Panquehue; granite and schist hillsides; coastal sites near Zapallar and Quillota with clay over schist and a strong Pacific influence.
cl-valle-del-aconcagua.nerd_note: 'Aconcagua Costa' and 'Aconcagua Andes' on Errázuriz labels are the 2011 complement terms in action, not separate appellations.
cl-valle-del-aconcagua.summary:
The Aconcagua Valley is where Chile's fine-wine revival found its first great red. In 1870 Maximiano Errázuriz planted French vines at Panquehue, about 100 km north of Santiago, on the warm inland floor of a valley that funnels Andean snowmelt from Aconcagua mountain to the sea at Concón. Panquehue's heat, which in the 1990s produced the Cabernet-Carmenère blend Seña and the Don Maximiano Founder's Reserve, made Aconcagua synonymous with dense, sun-built reds.

The valley is more varied than that. It runs from the Andean foothills (Calle Larga, San Esteban, Santa María), through the warm central basin of Panquehue, Catemu and Llaillay, to the coastal hills of Quillota, Hijuelas and Zapallar. Since 2005 Errázuriz has planted its Manzanar vineyard about 12 km from the Pacific, labelled Aconcagua Costa, where schist and clay soils give taut Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Seña moved its own vineyard to the Ocoa hills of Hijuelas, a biodynamic hillside between the two climates.

Taste the contrast: Panquehue Cabernet and Syrah are broad and ripe, Aconcagua Costa whites are saline and lean, and the 2004 Berlin Tasting, where Viñedo Chadwick 2000 and Seña 2001 beat first-growth Bordeaux blind, put the whole valley on the world map.

cl-valle-del-bio-bio.name: Valle del Bío-Bío
cl-valle-del-bio-bio.grapes: País, Moscatel de Alejandría, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Sauvignon Blanc
cl-valle-del-bio-bio.summary: The Bío-Bío subregion follows Chile's second-longest river in the old frontier country of southern Chile: Yumbel, Nacimiento, Mulchén, Negrete and Laja communes. For centuries it made País and Moscatel for local consumption; since the 1990s cooler, wetter conditions (well over 1,000 mm of rain) have drawn Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Gewürztraminer and Sauvignon Blanc. Its two areas are Yumbel and Mulchén. In July 2026 the Secano Interior special DO was extended to seven Biobío communes, including Nacimiento, Los Ángeles and Laja, in recognition of the region's peasant wine tradition.

cl-valle-del-cachapoal.name: Valle del Cachapoal
cl-valle-del-cachapoal.summary:
Cachapoal is the northern zone of Rapel, following the Cachapoal river from the Andes past Rancagua to Lake Rapel. Its east, under the mountains (Requínoa, Machalí, Rengo), is Cabernet country, home to Altaïr and the Andes-side vineyards of Viña San Pedro. Its west, around Peumo, Pichidegua and Las Cabras, is the warm, sheltered bowl where Chilean Carmenère reaches its fullest, ripest form: Concha y Toro's Carmín de Peumo and Terrunyo Carmenère come from here.

Before 1994 Chileans called the late-ripening vine here 'Merlot Peumal' after the Peumo valley, and the name stuck as a nickname for Carmenère. The area also hides Vik in Millahue, a showpiece estate with a winery built over water. In the glass, Peumo Carmenère is plush and spicy with dark fruit, and Andes-side Cabernet is firmer and fresher.

cl-valle-del-cautin.name: Valle del Cautín
cl-valle-del-cautin.summary: Cautín, matching Perquenco and Galvarino communes in Araucanía, is a small, very cool subregion where a few producers grow Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc on volcanic soils under heavy rainfall. It is part of the push of Chilean viticulture into the lake district.

cl-valle-del-choapa.name: Valle del Choapa
cl-valle-del-choapa.summary: The Choapa Valley, about 400 km north of Santiago, is where Chile is narrowest and the Andes and coastal range almost touch. It has two areas, Illapel and Salamanca, few vineyards and almost no wineries of its own; grapes grown on rocky foothill soils here, mainly Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon, are trucked south to wineries elsewhere, prized for high acidity and low pH.

cl-valle-del-claro.name: Valle del Claro
cl-valle-del-claro.summary: Claro is the northern zone of Maule, named after the river through Talca: Talca, San Clemente, Pencahue, Maule, Pelarco, San Rafael, Empedrado and Curepto communes. It runs from Andean San Clemente to the coastal slate of Empedrado.

cl-valle-del-elqui.name: Valle del Elqui
cl-valle-del-elqui.grapes: Syrah, Carmenère, Sauvignon Blanc, Pedro Jiménez; Moscatel and Pedro Jiménez for pisco
cl-valle-del-elqui.terroir: Granite and colluvial soils on steep valley sides; strong UV, very low humidity and big day-night swings at altitude; the coastal end is cooled by the Pacific fog called *camanchaca*.
cl-valle-del-elqui.nerd_note: Falernia's founders came from Trentino in Italy and named the estate after Falernian, the most famous wine of ancient Rome.
cl-valle-del-elqui.summary:
The Elqui Valley, about 500 km north of Santiago, is one of the clearest skies on Earth (hence its observatories) and the spiritual home of Chilean pisco. Vineyards climb from the coast near La Serena to around 2,000 m in the side valleys above Vicuña and Paiguano, and since Viña Falernia began bottling in the late 1990s the valley has shown that Syrah grown in intense light and cold nights can be peppery, floral and fresh rather than jammy. Rainfall is under 100 mm a year, so every vine is drip-irrigated with snowmelt from the Elqui river.

Most of the valley's grapes still go to pisco, especially Moscatel and Pedro Jiménez, and the town of Pisco Elqui renamed itself in 1936 to stake Chile's claim in the long dispute with Peru over the name. For wine drinkers the interest lies in the extremes: Sauvignon Blanc and Syrah from wind-cooled sites near the coast, and high-altitude Syrah, Garnacha and Carignan from the granitic slopes of Paiguano and Alcohuaz.

cl-valle-del-huasco.name: Valle del Huasco
cl-valle-del-huasco.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah; Moscatel for pisco and pajarete
cl-valle-del-huasco.nerd_note: Tara's coastal vineyard gets almost no rain at all: the vines live on fog, drip lines and stubbornness.
cl-valle-del-huasco.summary: Subregion matching Huasco province, where the Huasco river cuts from the Andes to the sea past Vallenar and Freirina. The upper valley around Alto del Carmen is pisco and *pajarete* country (a traditional sweet wine made from concentrated must); the coastal end has become a laboratory for desert-coast viticulture, where Viña Ventisquero's Tara project grows Chardonnay and Pinot Noir on saline, calcareous soils a few kilometres from the Pacific.

cl-valle-del-itata.name: Valle del Itata
cl-valle-del-itata.grapes: País, Cinsault, Moscatel de Alejandría, Carignan, Semillon, Corinto (Chasselas)
cl-valle-del-itata.terroir: Decomposed granite (*maicillo*) and red clay on rolling coastal hills; humid Mediterranean climate with 1,000 mm or more of winter rain; dry-farmed, own-rooted bush vines.
cl-valle-del-itata.nerd_note: Itata's Moscatel is the same Muscat of Alexandria distilled into pisco further north; here it is fermented dry, often on its skins.
cl-valle-del-itata.summary:
Itata is where Chilean wine began in earnest and where its oldest living vineyards remain. Spanish settlers and Jesuits planted vines around Concepción and Chillán in the mid-16th century, and by the colonial era the Itata and Ñuble river country supplied wine to Concepción and beyond; one shipment of 5,000 *botijas* went from Concepción to Lima in 1795. Phylloxera never came, so head-trained País, Moscatel de Alejandría and Cinsault still grow on their own roots on granite hills a few kilometres from the Pacific.

For most of the 20th century Itata sold cheap bulk wine to the big Central Valley houses. That changed in the 2010s, when De Martino, Carmen, Pedro Parra, Roberto Henríquez, Leonardo Erazo and many small farmers started bottling dry-farmed Cinsault and País of real charm: bright red fruit, light body, granite-dust freshness. Moscatel became a fragrant dry white and the base of skin-contact orange wines. The 2018 creation of the Ñuble administrative region gave Itata a political identity too, and SAG's 2024 census counted about 10,300 ha of wine grapes in Ñuble.

The subregion covers coastal and central Ñuble plus Florida commune; its four areas are Chillán, Quillón, Portezuelo and Coelemu. Much of it is also covered by the Secano Interior special DO for País and Cinsault, and in 2022 Itata growers protested a plan to open those two grapes to every Chilean DO, fearing they would lose the one advantage they had.

cl-valle-del-limari.name: Valle del Limarí
cl-valle-del-limari.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Syrah
cl-valle-del-limari.terroir: Calcareous clays and limestone in the coastal hills (Talinay, Quebrada Seca), alluvial terraces along the river, granite inland; persistent morning fog, strong afternoon winds and almost no rain.
cl-valle-del-limari.nerd_note: Quebrada Seca, Limarí's best-known Chardonnay site, was refused its own DO in 2018 because it is not a recognised named locality, only a dry gully.
cl-valle-del-limari.summary:
Limarí, about 400 km north of Santiago, holds something almost unique in Chile: limestone. Calcium carbonate deposits in the coastal hills of Talinay and Quebrada Seca, a rarity in a country of granite and alluvium, give Limarí Chardonnay a salty, chalky tension that winemakers compare to Chablis without blushing. The Pacific is only 20 to 30 km away and the morning *camanchaca* fog rolls up the valley daily, so this desert edge (under 100 mm of rain) behaves like a cool-climate region.

Vines were planted here in colonial times, but the modern story begins in the 1990s with Tabalí, Concha y Toro's Maycas del Limarí project and De Martino scouting for new terroir. Chardonnay is the headline, with Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and cool, savoury Syrah close behind. Inland, in Monte Patria and Río Hurtado, the valley is warmer and drier and still mostly devoted to pisco and table grapes.

cl-valle-del-loncomilla.name: Valle del Loncomilla
cl-valle-del-loncomilla.summary: Loncomilla is the central zone of Maule, along the Loncomilla river: San Javier, Villa Alegre, Retiro, Parral, Linares, Yerbas Buenas, Colbún and Longaví communes. It mixes large irrigated estates with the old dry-farmed Carignan and País of the western hills around San Javier and Villa Alegre.

cl-valle-del-lontue.name: Valle del Lontué
cl-valle-del-lontue.summary: Lontué is the southern zone of Curicó, along the Lontué river: Curicó, Molina and Sagrada Familia communes plus Río Claro in Talca province. It is the valley's productive centre, with large estates around Molina and Lontué.

cl-valle-del-maipo.name: Valle del Maipo
cl-valle-del-maipo.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Franc; some Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc
cl-valle-del-maipo.terroir: Stony alluvial terraces of the Maipo river (Puente Alto's 'piedmont' gravels), colluvial fans at the foot of the Andes, warmer clay-loams in the centre and granitic coastal hills in the west; Mediterranean climate, about 300 to 350 mm of winter rain, cold Andean night winds.
cl-valle-del-maipo.nerd_note: 'Alto Maipo' is not a legal name: on labels the Andean sector shows up through the area names Puente Alto and Pirque, or through the complement *Andes*.
cl-valle-del-maipo.summary:
Maipo is the historic heart of Chilean fine wine and the home of its most famous Cabernet Sauvignon. When Santiago's 19th-century mining and banking aristocracy came home from Paris, they planted Bordeaux varieties on their estates at the city's edge: Silvestre Ochagavía imported French vines and a French winemaker in 1851, Cousiño Macul was founded in 1856, Santa Carolina in 1875, Santa Rita in 1880 and Concha y Toro at Pirque in 1883. Those estates, a short carriage ride from the capital, defined the Chilean style for a century.

The subregion covers the whole Metropolitan Region, from the Andean foothills to the coastal range, and growers split it three ways. Alto Maipo, on the Andean piedmont at 600 to 800 m (Puente Alto, Pirque, Santiago's Macul and Peñalolén), has stony alluvial terraces of the Maipo river and cold mountain air at night; it gives Chile's classic Cabernet, with cassis, graphite and the hint of mint or eucalyptus locals call the Maipo signature. Central Maipo (Buin, Paine, Isla de Maipo, Talagante) is warmer and flatter, a source of generous Cabernet and Carmenère. Pacific Maipo, towards Melipilla and Alhué, feels the sea breeze and is the newest frontier.

The wines to know come mostly from a 10 km stretch of Puente Alto: Don Melchor (first vintage 1987), Almaviva (the 1997 Concha y Toro and Baron Philippe de Rothschild joint venture) and Viñedo Chadwick, whose 2000 vintage won the 2004 Berlin Tasting. Maipo Cabernet is firmer and more savoury than Napa's, more sun-filled than Bordeaux, and among the best-value long-agers in the world.

cl-valle-del-malleco.name: Valle del Malleco
cl-valle-del-malleco.terroir: Volcanic soils (trumao) of sand and clay, well drained despite heavy rain; cool, short season with big day-night swings.
cl-valle-del-malleco.nerd_note: Aquitania's founding partners included Bordeaux's Bruno Prats and Paul Pontallier, so Chile's southern Chardonnay pioneer has Médoc roots.
cl-valle-del-malleco.summary: Malleco, about 550 km south of Santiago in Araucanía, is the subregion that proved southern Chile could make world-class white wine. In the mid-1990s Felipe de Solminihac of Viña Aquitania planted Chardonnay near Traiguén on well-drained volcanic soils; the resulting Sol de Sol Chardonnay, first released around 2000, showed a nervy, citrus-and-flint style no one expected from Chile. Rainfall reaches about 1,300 mm a year, the season is short and frost is a constant threat, so yields are tiny. Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc follow the same cool logic. The single defined area is Traiguén.

cl-valle-del-marga-marga.name: Valle del Marga-Marga
cl-valle-del-marga-marga.summary: A small coastal subregion matching Quilpué commune, inland from Viña del Mar, listed directly under the Aconcagua region. It is cool, hilly and close to the sea, with only a few vineyards, mostly for white wine and Pinot Noir. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-valle-del-maule.name: Valle del Maule
cl-valle-del-maule.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Carmenère, Chardonnay, País, Carignan, Cinsault, Malbec
cl-valle-del-maule.terroir: Volcanic and alluvial soils on the irrigated valley floor; granite, decomposed granite (*maicillo*) and slate on the dry-farmed coastal hills; cooler and wetter than the Maipo, with about 700 mm of rain.
cl-valle-del-maule.nerd_note: VIGNO wines must be at least 65% Carignan from dry-farmed vines over 30 years old in Maule's secano and spend at least two years ageing before release; the rules are a private association's, not part of Decree 464.
cl-valle-del-maule.summary:
Maule is Chile's biggest wine subregion by far. SAG's 2024 census put 48,565 ha of wine grapes in the Maule administrative region (which also contains Curicó), 41.5% of the national total, and in 2026 that administrative region made 452 million litres, about 48% of all Chilean wine. Much of that is bulk Cabernet, Sauvignon Blanc and Merlot from irrigated valley floor; but Maule also holds the country's deepest well of history. Spanish settlers planted País here in the 16th century, and on the dry-farmed granite hills of the coastal range, the *secano*, head-trained bush vines of País, Carignan and Cinsault, some well over a century old, survived every modernisation simply because nobody bothered to rip them out.

The decree splits Maule into three zones. Claro (around Talca) runs from Andean San Clemente to coastal Empedrado and Curepto, where slate soils give rare mineral reds. Loncomilla (Linares, San Javier, Parral, Villa Alegre, Colbún) is the warm central valley plus the old Carignan of the dry hills. Tutuvén is the single area of Cauquenes, the epicentre of dry-farmed País and Carignan.

Since about 2010 the VIGNO (Vignadores de Carignan) association has defined a Maule Carignan style from old, dry-farmed bush vines, and a new generation (Bouchon, Gillmore, González Bastías, Garage Wine Co, De Martino and many more) bottles País and Cinsault that taste of wild strawberry, earth and dust. Maule is where Chile reconnects with its first four centuries of wine.

cl-valle-del-rapel.name: Valle del Rapel
cl-valle-del-rapel.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc
cl-valle-del-rapel.summary: The Rapel subregion covers the O'Higgins administrative region, named after the Rapel river that forms where the Cachapoal and Tinguiririca join. It contains two zones, Cachapoal to the north and Colchagua to the south, and SAG figures show O'Higgins making about 282 million litres of DO wine in 2026, second only to Maule. 'Valle del Rapel' alone on a label usually means a blend across both zones; serious bottles name Cachapoal, Colchagua or an area.

cl-valle-del-teno.name: Valle del Teno
cl-valle-del-teno.summary: Teno is the northern zone of Curicó, along the Teno river and the Mataquito towards the coast: Teno, Romeral, Rauco, Hualañé and Vichuquén communes. It runs from Andean piedmont at Romeral through warm valley floor to coastal hills near Lake Vichuquén.

cl-valle-del-tutuven.name: Valle del Tutuvén
cl-valle-del-tutuven.summary: Tutuvén is Maule's southern-coastal zone, consisting only of Cauquenes commune, named after the Tutuvén river. It is the heart of Chile's dry-farmed old-vine country.

cl-vichuquen.name: Vichuquén
cl-vichuquen.summary: Area matching Vichuquén commune on the coast around Lake Vichuquén, with new cool-climate plantings of Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

cl-vicuna.name: Vicuña
cl-vicuna.summary: Area matching Vicuña commune, the heart of the middle Elqui valley and home of Viña Falernia, where wide valley-floor vineyards sit at around 500 to 700 m between bare granite mountains. Syrah and Carmenère ripen easily in the intense sun; the nights, cooled by air draining off the Andes, keep the wines aromatic. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

cl-villa-alegre.name: Villa Alegre
cl-villa-alegre.summary: Area matching Villa Alegre commune south of Talca, with vineyards on the Loncomilla plain and old secano vines nearby. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-yumbel.name: Yumbel
cl-yumbel.summary: Area defined by Yumbel and Laja communes on the north bank of the Bío-Bío, an old frontier town famous for its San Sebastián pilgrimage; dry-farmed País here qualifies for Secano Interior. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

cl-zapallar.name: Zapallar
cl-zapallar.summary: Area matching Zapallar commune on the Pacific coast north of Valparaíso, listed in the decree directly under the Aconcagua region. A handful of new coastal vineyards here grow Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah in fog and sea wind; it marks the northern edge of Aconcagua's coastal frontier. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

sites.name: Viña Concha y Toro, Pirque
sites.text: Founded in 1883 by Melchor de Concha y Toro and his wife Emiliana Subercaseaux at their country house in Pirque, on the south bank of the Maipo. Today it is Latin America's largest wine company, and the historic park, house and the 'Casillero del Diablo' cellar (named for a legend the founder spread to scare off thieves) are Chile's most visited wine attraction.

sites.name: Don Melchor vineyard
sites.text: A Cabernet vineyard of about 127 ha on the alluvial terrace of the Maipo at Puente Alto, source of Don Melchor since its first vintage in 1987. Farmed in soil-defined blocks of river stones and sandy loam, it is the benchmark for Puente Alto Cabernet: cassis, cedar and graphite with fine, firm tannin. Now run as an independent winery within the Concha y Toro group.

sites.name: Almaviva
sites.text: Created in 1997 by Concha y Toro and Baron Philippe de Rothschild (Mouton) to make one Bordeaux-style blend from Puente Alto, with Carmenère as a distinctive minor partner. The wine's name, from Count Almaviva of Beaumarchais and Mozart's *Le nozze di Figaro*, and its single-wine focus signalled Chile's arrival among the great Cabernet terroirs.

sites.name: Viñedo Chadwick
sites.text: Eduardo Chadwick planted this 15-ha Cabernet vineyard in 1992 on his father's former polo field in Puente Alto. Its 2000 vintage beat Lafite, Margaux and Latour in the 2004 Berlin Tasting, and its 2014 vintage became the first Chilean wine to receive a perfect 100-point score from James Suckling.

sites.name: Viña Santa Rita, Alto Jahuel
sites.text: Founded in 1880 by Domingo Fernández Concha in Alto Jahuel, Buin. During the War of Independence its hacienda sheltered 120 soldiers of Bernardo O'Higgins, celebrated in the '120' wine range. The estate keeps a colonial house, chapel, park and the Andean Museum of pre-Columbian art.

sites.name: Viña Cousiño Macul, Peñalolén
sites.text: Founded in 1856 by Matías Cousiño, whose family fortune came from coal and silver, on land at the foot of the Andes in what is now Santiago's Peñalolén. Its 19th-century brick cellars are among the oldest in Chile; urban growth has shrunk the vineyard, and most production moved to Buin, but the historic winery still operates inside the city.

sites.name: Viña Carmen, Alto Jahuel
sites.text: Chile's oldest wine brand (1850) and the place where, on 24 November 1994, the French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot noticed that some of the 'Merlot' vines were in fact Carmenère, a grape thought lost after phylloxera. Viña Carmen's neighbouring estate sits in Alto Jahuel, Buin, close to Santa Rita.

sites.name: Viña Santa Carolina, Macul
sites.text: Founded in 1875 by Luis Pereira and named after his wife Carolina Íñiguez. Its 19th-century cellars, built with lime and egg-white mortar, survive inside Santiago's Macul district and are a national monument; Macul lies just outside the decree's 'Santiago' area, within the wider Maipo subregion.

sites.name: Viña Aquitania, Peñalolén
sites.text: Founded in 1990 by Bordeaux's Bruno Prats (Cos d'Estournel) and Paul Pontallier (Château Margaux) with Chilean Felipe de Solminihac, on the last Andean foothill vineyards inside Santiago. Its Lazuli Cabernet comes from here; its Sol de Sol Chardonnay from Malleco.

sites.name: Haras de Pirque
sites.text: A thoroughbred horse stud turned winery in Pirque, its horseshoe-shaped gravity cellar set among hillside Cabernet vineyards at the mouth of the Maipo canyon. Italy's Antinori family, first its partner in the Albis blend, later took control of the estate.

sites.name: Antiyal, Paine
sites.text: Álvaro Espinoza's family estate in Paine, one of Chile's pioneers of biodynamic farming from the late 1990s. A tiny vineyard of Carmenère, Cabernet and Syrah tended with cows, compost and lunar calendars.

sites.name: De Martino, Isla de Maipo
sites.text: The De Martino family winery (founded 1934) led Chile's 2010s turn away from ripeness and new oak. Its Viejas Tinajas wines from Itata, fermented in old clay jars, and its single-vineyard Legado range map terroirs from Limarí to Malleco.

sites.name: Viña Undurraga, Talagante
sites.text: Francisco Undurraga founded the winery in 1885 at Santa Ana, Talagante, where its historic house and landscaped park survive. Undurraga says it was the first Chilean winery to export to the United States, in 1903.

sites.name: Viña Errázuriz, Panquehue
sites.text: Maximiano Errázuriz planted the Aconcagua Valley's first fine-wine vineyard here in 1870. Today the Chadwick family's Errázuriz runs the historic bodega, the hillside Max Viñedo, the Don Maximiano Founder's Reserve vineyard and a modern icon winery built in 2010.

sites.name: Max Viñedo (Errázuriz)
sites.text: The terraced hillside vineyard above Errázuriz's Panquehue bodega, source of Don Maximiano and the Max range. Colluvial slopes on the warm north side of the Aconcagua valley give ripe but structured Cabernet, Carmenère and Syrah.

sites.name: Seña
sites.text: Conceived in 1995 by Eduardo Chadwick and Robert Mondavi as Chile's first icon blend. After early vintages from Panquehue, the wine moved to its own biodynamic hillside vineyard in the Ocoa hills of Hijuelas, planted from 1998. Seña 2001 finished second in the 2004 Berlin Tasting.

sites.name: Manzanar vineyard, Aconcagua Costa
sites.text: Errázuriz's coastal vineyard about 12 km from the Pacific, planted from 2005 on schist and clay slopes. Labelled Aconcagua Costa, its Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah turned a valley famous for heat into a source of saline, cool-climate wine.

sites.name: Viña Veramonte, Casablanca
sites.text: Founded in 1990 by Agustín Huneeus at the eastern gateway of the Casablanca Valley on Ruta 68. One of the valley's first large estates, now farmed organically, known for Sauvignon Blanc and the Primus red blend.

sites.name: Casas del Bosque, Casablanca
sites.text: Founded in 1993 by the Cúneo family in the cooler western part of Casablanca, a few kilometres closer to the ocean than Ruta 68. Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir from frost-prone, granite-and-clay slopes.

sites.name: Kingston Family Vineyards
sites.text: The Kingston family, Americans who came to Chile to prospect for gold in the early 1900s, ran cattle in western Casablanca before planting vines in 1998. Their hillside Pinot Noir and Syrah sit among the coolest sites in the valley, in the western hills closest to the Pacific.

sites.name: Viña Leyda
sites.text: In 1998 the Fernández family ran an 8 km pipeline from the Maipo river to irrigate the dry hills of Leyda and planted the first vines in what became the Valle de Leyda zone. Leyda Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir now define the San Antonio coast's saline style.

sites.name: Casa Marín, Lo Abarca
sites.text: María Luz Marín planted vines 4 km from the Pacific at Lo Abarca in 2000, told by everyone that grapes would never ripen. Her single-slope Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir and Syrah gave the hamlet its own DO in 2018, practically a one-producer appellation.

sites.name: Matetic
sites.text: The Matetic family's biodynamic estate in the Rosario valley straddles the Casablanca and San Antonio boundary. Its EQ Syrah, from cool granite slopes, helped prove Chile could make peppery, Rhône-like Syrah.

sites.name: Viña Falernia, Vicuña
sites.text: Founded in 1998 by Aldo Olivier Gramola and his cousin Giorgio Flessati, Trentino natives, beside the Puclaro reservoir in the Elqui Valley. Falernia showed that the pisco valley could make serious wine, above all a peppery, high-altitude Syrah.

sites.name: Pisco Elqui
sites.text: A village in the upper Elqui (Paiguano) that changed its name from La Unión to Pisco Elqui in 1936 to assert Chile's claim to the word pisco in the long dispute with Peru. Distilleries and small vineyards of Moscatel and Pedro Jiménez line the river.

sites.name: Alcohuaz
sites.text: A hamlet at the top of the Claro valley in Paiguano where Viñedos de Alcohuaz farms terraced granite vineyards at roughly 1,700 to 2,200 m, among the highest in Chile. Syrah, Garnacha, Malbec and Petite Sirah are fermented in open stone lagares.

sites.name: Viña Tabalí, Limarí
sites.text: Tabalí's winery stands among petroglyphs in the Valle del Encanto near Ovalle. In the coastal hills of Talinay, about 12 km from the sea, its vineyards grow on limestone, a geological rarity in Chile, giving taut, salty Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Talinay hills, Limarí
sites.text: The coastal Altos de Talinay, where Tabalí planted on calcium carbonate soils in the 2000s. The limestone and the daily camanchaca fog make this one of the few places in South America where Chardonnay tastes of chalk.

sites.name: Quebrada Seca, Limarí
sites.text: A dry gully in the lower Limarí with calcareous soils, source of Concha y Toro's Maycas del Limarí and other mineral Chardonnays. It was proposed as a DO in 2018 but refused because it is not a recognised named locality.

sites.name: Clos Apalta (Lapostolle)
sites.text: Alexandra Marnier-Lapostolle (of the Grand Marnier family) and Cyril de Bournet founded Lapostolle in 1994. Its Clos Apalta, a Carmenère-led blend from old vines in the Apalta horseshoe, is made in a multi-level gravity winery cut into the granite hill, completed in 2005.

sites.name: Viña Montes, Apalta
sites.text: Aurelio Montes and partners founded Montes in 1987 and built a feng-shui-inspired gravity winery in Apalta, where Gregorian chant plays to barrels. Montes Alpha M (1996) and Folly, Chile's first Syrah from Apalta's steepest slopes, made the hillside famous.

sites.name: Montes Folly vineyard
sites.text: The steep upper slopes of Apalta where Montes planted Syrah in the 1990s, against local advice that vines could not be farmed on 45-degree granite. The 'folly' produced Chile's first icon Syrah, Montes Folly.

sites.name: Neyen, Apalta
sites.text: An old adobe estate in the eastern Apalta horseshoe with Carmenère and Cabernet vines over a century old. Its single blend, Espíritu de Apalta, shows the valley's dark fruit and granite freshness.

sites.name: Viña Ventisquero, Apalta
sites.text: Ventisquero's Apalta vineyard produces Pangea Syrah, created with the Australian winemaker John Duval, formerly of Penfolds Grange. The same company runs the pioneering Tara desert-coast project in the Huasco valley of Atacama.

sites.name: Museo de Colchagua, Santa Cruz
sites.text: Chile's largest private museum, founded by Carlos Cardoen in Santa Cruz in 1995, with collections from pre-Columbian ceramics to colonial winemaking tools, wine presses and huaso culture. It anchors the Colchagua wine route.

sites.name: Hacienda Los Lingues
sites.text: One of Chile's oldest colonial estates, granted in the 16th century and owned by the same family for centuries, famous for its Aculeo horses and old manor. It gave its name to the 492-ha Los Lingues DO, upheld by Chile's Supreme Court in June 2026.

sites.name: Casa Silva, Angostura
sites.text: The Silva family, which traces its Colchagua winemaking to a French ancestor in the 1890s, runs this estate near San Fernando with its own polo field and hotel. Casa Silva pioneered coastal Paredones and the far-south Lago Ranco vineyard in Osorno.

sites.name: Los Vascos, Peralillo
sites.text: A colonial Basque-founded estate bought in 1988 by Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite), one of the first foreign investments of Chile's modern era. Its Le Dix blend marked the tenth anniversary of the partnership.

sites.name: Viña Vik, Millahue
sites.text: Norwegian-Uruguayan Alexander Vik's estate in the Millahue valley of Cachapoal, chosen after a lengthy terroir study. The winery sits beneath a stretched fabric roof over a water-covered cellar, next to a dramatic hilltop hotel.

sites.name: Concha y Toro Peumo vineyard
sites.text: The Peumo vineyard on the Cachapoal river, source of Carmín de Peumo and Terrunyo Carmenère. Clay-rich alluvial soils and a warm, sheltered bowl let Carmenère ripen fully, which is why Chilean growers once called the grape 'Merlot Peumal'.

sites.name: Miguel Torres, Curicó
sites.text: Miguel A. Torres bought land in Curicó in 1979, the first foreign winery investment of Chile's modern era. Stainless steel and temperature-controlled fermentation followed, and today Torres also works with Maule's País and Empedrado's slate.

sites.name: Viña San Pedro, Molina
sites.text: Founded in 1865, San Pedro farms one of the largest single vineyard blocks in South America at Lontué, Molina. It anchors the VSPT group and the 1865 and Altaïr labels.

sites.name: Viña Gillmore, San Javier
sites.text: A family estate in Villavicencio, San Javier, in the dry-farmed hills of Loncomilla, with old Carignan, Cabernet Franc and País. Gillmore is a member of VIGNO and a strong voice for Maule's old vines.

sites.name: J. Bouchon, Mingre
sites.text: The Bouchon family, from Bordeaux in the 1890s, farms Maule's coastal secano at Mingre, where they rescued wild País vines climbing trees and dry-farmed old Carignan and Semillon.

sites.name: Cauquenes secano vineyards
sites.text: The granite hills around Cauquenes hold Chile's densest concentration of dry-farmed, head-trained País and Carignan, many vines a century or more old, ploughed by horse and never irrigated. This is the heartland of VIGNO and of the Secano Interior special DO.

sites.name: Guarilihue, Itata
sites.text: A granite hamlet in Coelemu, 20 km from the sea, with own-rooted Cinsault and Moscatel planted generations ago. De Martino's Viejas Tinajas and many small producers' Cinsaults come from here, fermented in old clay tinajas.

sites.name: Traiguén (Sol de Sol vineyard)
sites.text: Viña Aquitania planted Chardonnay near Traiguén in Malleco in the mid-1990s, in a cool, rainy corner of Araucanía. The result, Sol de Sol, was the first wine to show southern Chile's potential for tense, ageable Chardonnay.

sites.name: Lago Ranco vineyard (Casa Silva)
sites.text: Casa Silva's vineyard on the shore of Lake Ranco at Futrono, near 40°S, one of the southernmost in Chile. The lake moderates frost; Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and sparkling base wines carry very high natural acidity.
